Neonatal shortfin makos emerge from the mother at a total length of approximately 65 cm [Lb = approximately 65 cm], a size that equips them for a fast-swimming, pelagic lifestyle from the moment of birth. Their birth weight, recorded at roughly 2000 grams [Wwb = roughly 2000 grams], reflects an extended gestation period that allows for substantial pre-natal development. This gestational duration, estimated at 16.5 months under the typical thermal conditions of warm-temperate waters at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], corresponds to an age at birth of 16.5 months [ab = 16.5 months]. The combination of a large body size at parturition and an active, predatory habit gives these neonates a competitive edge in the open ocean, where prey detection and capture must commence almost immediately after birth. The yolk-sac is entirely resorbed prior to parturition, and the exotrophic transition is effectively instantaneous, as pups begin foraging on small teleost fishes and squid within their first few days of independent life. This strategy of producing relatively few, large offspring is consistent with the broader k-selected life history observed across the family Lamnidae.

Female shortfin makos attain a substantially greater ultimate total length than males, with adult females reaching up to 365 cm [Li = up to 365 cm] in total length, while the largest recorded males measure approximately 283 cm [Li = approximately 283 cm]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum size is accompanied by a comparable disparity in mass: females can achieve an ultimate wet weight of around 505,800 grams [Wwi = around 505,800 grams], whereas males typically cap out at about 201,500 grams [Wwi = about 201,500 grams]. Such differences are thought to reflect the high energetic demands of gestation and parturition in females, which select for larger body sizes capable of accommodating and nourishing developing embryos over a gestation period that can extend beyond a year. In contrast, male reproductive success is more tightly linked to mobility and the ability to locate receptive mates, which may favour a somewhat smaller, more agile body plan. These size estimates are derived from empirical measurements of both captured and commercially landed individuals across the species’ circumglobal range.

The onset of sexual maturity in shortfin makos occurs at markedly different sizes between the sexes. Under the thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], females generally reach puberty at a total length of around 300 cm [Lp = around 300 cm], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 200,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 200,000 grams]. Males mature considerably smaller, attaining puberty at roughly 201 cm [Lp = roughly 201 cm] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of about 130,000 grams [Wwp = about 130,000 grams]. The time since birth at which these milestones are reached also differs substantially: females require approximately 18 years since birth [tp = approximately 18 years since birth] to reach puberty, whereas males achieve sexual maturity in roughly 8 years since birth [tp = roughly 8 years since birth] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. These values, recorded in wild populations, highlight a life history characterised by delayed maturation, particularly in females, which may contribute to the species’ vulnerability to overfishing. The slower maturation schedule for females imposes a long pre-reproductive phase during which individuals are susceptible to anthropogenic mortality before they have contributed to the next generation.

Reproductive output in the shortfin mako is comparatively low, reflecting a strategy of producing a modest number of well-developed pups. Females give birth to litters ranging from 4 to 16 pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from 4 to 16 pups], with an estimated maximum reproductive rate that translates to approximately one litter every three years [F_R_i = approximately one litter every three years], as observed in populations inhabiting waters at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The maximum lifespan of this species under natural conditions is thought to be around 32 years [am = around 32 years], a relatively extended duration for a pelagic shark, which further underscores the slow pace of its life history at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The combination of late maturity, small litter sizes, and long inter-breeding intervals means that even modest increases in fishing mortality can have disproportionately severe impacts on population persistence. Age-based demographic models indicate that the species is particularly sensitive to the removal of mature females, given their key role in sustaining recruitment over time.

From a physiological perspective, the shortfin mako exhibits several adaptations that support its status as one of the ocean’s fastest pelagic sharks. Its regional endothermy, which allows it to maintain elevated body temperatures in cool water, is facilitated by a specialised vascular counter-current heat exchange system. This capacity for partial homeothermy enhances muscle performance and digestive efficiency, enabling the species to exploit a broad thermal niche. Comparative studies with other lamnid sharks, such as the white shark and the porbeagle, suggest that the mako’s metabolic rate is among the highest recorded for any elasmobranch, consistent with its active, pursuit-based predation on fast-moving prey including tunas, billfishes, and squids. The species also displays a remarkably high aerobic scope, which permits sustained swimming speeds of several kilometres per hour during migratory movements. These physiological traits, combined with its life history parameters, make the shortfin mako a striking example of evolutionary adaptation to the apex predator niche in pelagic ecosystems.
